1:
TEACHER NOTES:
This title slide opens Lesson 8. Have pencil, mini whiteboards, textas and booklets out before you click off this slide.
2:
TEACHER NOTES:
Planning slide for the teacher. The Extended Path is the 60 minute version. Use the full deck unless your time slot is shorter.
3:
TEACHER NOTES:
Pre-read the matching Teacher Handbook before teaching. This lesson focuses on characters, perspective, thought bubbles, comic strips and sentence types. The text is A Year on our Farm.
4:
TEACHER NOTES:
Quick icon reference. I = I do, W = We do, CfU = Check for understanding, Y = You do. Skip past for students.
5:
TEACHER NOTES:
Legend for student response routines used through the deck. Whiteboard response, choral response, thumbs and show fingers come up most often.
6:
TEACHER NOTES:
Icon legend only. No teaching action required.
7:
TEACHER NOTES:
Reference chart for the colour coded sentence parts. Use only if you plan to colour code parts of speech today.
8:
SAY:
- "We need three things on our desks."
- "Pencil. Mini whiteboard with a texta. Booklet."
- "Show me your texta up high when you are ready."

DO:
- Point to each item on the slide as students get it out.
- Wait until every student has all three before moving on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick set up slide. Do not start the character work until every student has a working board and texta.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with no texta or a dry texta. Top up before reading begins.
9:
TEACHER NOTES:
Divider for the character and creating text section. Use it to settle the class before slide 10. Eyes up before you click on.
10:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen first."
- "Characters are the people, animals or creatures in a story who can think, act and feel."
- "In A Year on our Farm, the characters are Mum, Dad, Jess, Georgie and the narrator who is not named."
- "Ask: who tells the story? Expected: the narrator, who does not have a name in the book."

DO:
- Point to each photo on the slide as you name the family member.
- Hold up the book cover so students can see who the family is.
- Tap the words think, act, feel as you say them.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the first I Do for character. The five characters listed are the family members and the narrator. Do not invent extra characters not on the slide or in the book.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who name the animals as the main characters. Set up slide 11 by saying "We will talk about the animals next."
11:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen."
- "Animals can be characters too, but in this story the animals do not talk or think like people."
- "They are an important part of the farm, but they are not characters in the same way as the family."

DO:
- Point to each animal photo on the slide.
- Tap the part of the slide that says "do not talk or think like people."
- Glance back at slide 10's family photos to compare.

TEACHER NOTES:
Key distinction for this story. Animals matter, but they are not full characters here because they do not talk or think in the book.

WATCH FOR:
- Students still wanting to call Maria the cat a character. Quick correction: "Maria is in the story, but she does not talk or think like a person."
12:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen."
- "Perspective means seeing things from another person's point of view."
- "We can ask a character a question and answer as if we were them."
- "Listen to me as the narrator. Question: What do you like most about farm life? Answer: I love when the lambs are born and I feel proud when I help Mum feed them."

DO:
- Point to the question and answer on the slide as you read each.
- Use a different voice for the narrator's answer to show role play.
- Tap the word perspective and repeat it.

TEACHER NOTES:
Introduces the word perspective. Keep it concrete: stepping into the character's shoes and answering as them. The slide gives a worked example with the narrator.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confused by the word perspective. Quick rephrase: "Pretending you are the character."
13:
SAY:
- "Turn and tell your partner."
- "What other questions could we ask the narrator?"
- "Use the questions on the slide for ideas: What do you do on the farm? What is the hardest part? How do you feel in winter? What are you proud of?"

DO:
- Read each example question aloud.
- Give 30 to 45 seconds of partner talk.
- Take 2 to 3 student questions to share with the class.

TEACHER NOTES:
Warm up for the hot seat on slide 14. Students come up with their own questions to ask the narrator.

WATCH FOR:
- Students asking yes or no questions only. Prompt: "Try a question that starts with what or how."
14:
SAY:
- "Watch this first."
- "Hot seat means pretending you are the character and answering questions as them."
- "I will be the narrator. Ask me a question."
- "Question: What do you do on the farm? Answer as narrator: I help pick fruit, I care for the animals, and I keep an eye on Georgie."
- "Question: What is the hardest part? Answer: There is always lots of work, and we rely on the weather, which can be tricky."

DO:
- Sit in a chair at the front to mark the hot seat.
- Use a different voice or hand gesture for in role talk.
- Take 2 to 3 student questions and answer in role.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is teacher modelling of the hot seat. Stay in role. Keep answers short and tied to what is in the book.

WATCH FOR:
- Students drifting into questions about other stories. Bring them back to A Year on our Farm.
15:
SAY:
- "Now your turn with a partner."
- "One of you is the narrator. The other asks the questions."
- "Use the questions on the slide or your own."
- "Then swap so both of you have a turn in the hot seat."

DO:
- Set a 2 minute timer for the first round.
- Walk among pairs and listen.
- Stop after 2 minutes and ask pairs to swap.

TEACHER NOTES:
First pair turn. Walk past each pair to spot students who freeze in role. Use the example answers on the slide to scaffold them.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Pick one question from the slide and rehearse the answer aloud before going into the hot seat.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Ask a follow up question after each answer, like "Why do you feel that way?"

WATCH FOR:
- Students answering as themselves, not in role. Prompt: "Answer like you are the narrator."
16:
SAY:
- "Turn and tell your partner."
- "What questions could we ask Mum from the story?"
- "Use the four questions on the slide for ideas: What do you like most? Do you have favourite animals? Are there jobs you do not like? What would you like people to know about your farm?"

DO:
- Read each example question aloud.
- Give 30 to 45 seconds of partner talk.
- Take 2 to 3 student questions to share.

TEACHER NOTES:
Moves the hot seat focus from the narrator to Mum. Students prepare questions before slide 17's role play.

WATCH FOR:
- Students writing questions that the book cannot answer. Quick reminder: "Use what we know about Mum from the story."
17:
SAY:
- "Now we hot seat as Mum."
- "One student volunteers to be Mum. The class asks the questions from slide 16."
- "Listen carefully. Is the answer giving Mum's perspective?"

DO:
- Sit a willing student in the hot seat chair.
- Read or take 2 to 3 student questions one at a time.
- After each answer, ask the class: "Did that answer sound like Mum?"

TEACHER NOTES:
A student takes the hot seat. The example answers on the slide are a guide for what good in role answers sound like. Coach gently if needed.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who give an answer about themselves, not Mum. Prompt: "Answer as if you are Mum."
18:
SAY:
- "Pair share or small group."
- "Pick a character. Use cue cards or your own questions."
- "Take turns being in the hot seat."

DO:
- Hand out cue cards with sample questions if you have prepared them.
- Set a 4 to 5 minute timer.
- Walk between pairs and prompt students who freeze.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the active practice slide. Cue cards are mentioned on the slide but are not supplied with the deck, so prepare them in advance from the questions on slides 13 and 16, or let students use their own.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Use the question and answer pairs on slides 14 and 17 as a script first.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Ask a question that is not on any slide and try to answer in role.

WATCH FOR:
- Pairs who finish very quickly. Prompt them to swap roles or pick a new character.
19:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "What could the narrator say about what they do on the farm?"
- "Pick all the answers that fit."

DO:
- Read each option aloud once.
- Cue silent think, then fingers up.
- Reveal: I help pick apricots, I look after some of the animals, I help collect the eggs.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which answers fit what the narrator does on the farm? Expected: I help pick apricots, I look after animals, I help collect eggs.
- Scan for: most students picking the three farm based answers and rejecting the beach answer.
PROCEED:
- >=80% correct. Move to slide 20.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students pick "He helps his brother" because it sounds farm related.
- Reteach: "He helps his brother" is in third person, not first. The narrator answers as I, not he.
- Re-check: ask "How does the narrator start the sentence about themselves?"

TEACHER NOTES:
Key check that students understand first person voice in the hot seat. Two distractors: building sand castles on the beach (wrong setting) and "He helps his brother" (third person, not first).

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing the beach option. Quick correction: "This story is on a farm, not a beach."
20:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen first."
- "A thought bubble shows what a character is thinking."
- "It comes out of the character's head."
- "Look at the example: the character is thinking, I feel a bit scared because Vanessa is broody, but I love seeing her chicks when they hatch."

DO:
- Trace the shape of a thought bubble in the air.
- Point to the bubble on the slide and read the text inside it.
- Tap the word thinking each time.

TEACHER NOTES:
Introduces thought bubbles. The student-friendly idea is: a thought bubble shows what is in someone's head. Brood and broody may need a brief gloss for some students.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing speech bubbles and thought bubbles. Quick reminder: thought bubbles show thinking, not talking.
21:
SAY:
- "Look at Georgie on the slide."
- "What could Georgie be thinking? What could go in his thought bubble?"
- "Turn and tell your partner."

DO:
- Read the example on the slide: I feel happy because I love the tickly feeling of the chicks when I hold them.
- Give 30 to 45 seconds of partner talk.
- Take 2 to 3 student responses.

TEACHER NOTES:
Guided practice for thought bubbles. Use the example as a model. Push students to give a thought that fits Georgie in this story.

WATCH FOR:
- Students giving a thought that does not fit Georgie. Prompt: "What would Georgie think on the farm?"
22:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "Which other answers could go in Georgie's thought bubble?"
- "Pick all that fit."

DO:
- Read each option aloud.
- Cue silent think, then fingers up.
- Reveal: Apricots are delicious! I found a stinky rotten egg. I like helping on the farm.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which thoughts fit Georgie? Expected: Apricots are delicious! I found a stinky rotten egg. I like helping on the farm.
- Scan for: most students choosing the three farm based thoughts and rejecting the elephant and the name change.
PROCEED:
- >=80% correct. Move to the booklet task on slide 23.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students pick the elephant or the name option because they look fun.
- Reteach: "Is there an elephant on the farm? No. Is the boy's name Max? No, it is Georgie."
- Re-check: ask "What are some real things Georgie does in the story?"

TEACHER NOTES:
Final check on character thoughts before the booklet task. Two non-examples: a pet elephant and a different name.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick the elephant. Quick correction: "There is no elephant in the story."
23:
SAY:
- "Open your booklet to Lesson 8: Understanding, responding to and creating text."
- "Draw the face of a character from the story."
- "Then fill in the thought bubble to show what they are thinking."

DO:
- Wait until every student has the right page open.
- Read the task heading aloud once.
- Circulate to support students who are stuck on which character to choose.

TEACHER NOTES:
First booklet task. Students draw a face and add a thought bubble for one character. Use slides 20 to 22 as references.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Pick the narrator and copy one short thought from slide 14 or 19.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Write two thought bubbles for the same character at two different moments in the story.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write a thought that does not fit the chosen character. Prompt: "What would this person feel on the farm?"
24:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen first."
- "A comic strip is a short story told in pictures and words."
- "It has panels, which are boxes that show what happens step by step."
- "A three panel comic has three boxes: beginning, middle and end."
- "Each panel can have thought bubbles or speech bubbles. It can also have labels."

DO:
- Hold up three fingers to show beginning, middle, end.
- Tap the words panels, thought bubbles, speech bubbles, labels as you say them.

TEACHER NOTES:
Introduces comic strips. New words: panels, speech bubble, label. Students will have already met thought bubbles on slide 20.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who confuse a comic with a picture book. Quick reminder: comics use panels in order, like steps.
25:
SAY:
- "Look at this comic strip about Jess."
- "In the first panel, Jess thinks: I hope Vanessa is friendly so I can collect some eggs."
- "In the next panel, Jess thinks: I feel nervous because the eggs are fragile."
- "At the end, Jess thinks: Hooray! What could I make with this egg?"
- "Each panel shows a different moment."

DO:
- Point to each panel one by one.
- Read each thought bubble in order.
- Tap the boundary of each panel to show beginning, middle, end.

TEACHER NOTES:
Worked example showing how thoughts change across the three panels. Note for the teacher: this image was created using AI, as marked on the slide.

WATCH FOR:
- Students reading panels out of order. Slow down and point to each one in turn.
26:
SAY:
- "Here is the same idea, but with labels and a title."
- "A label tells us what is happening in the panel."
- "A title tells us the topic of the comic."

DO:
- Point to the title at the top of the comic.
- Point to each label under the panels.
- Compare to slide 25 by gesture.

TEACHER NOTES:
Adds the idea of titles and labels to the comic strip layout. Note for the teacher: this image was also created using AI.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing a label with a thought bubble. Quick reminder: a label is outside the panel, a thought bubble is inside.
27:
SAY:
- "Turn to page 10 of the text."
- "Look at Georgie finding the rotten egg."
- "Turn and tell your partner. What could go in each panel of a comic?"
- "Use the three steps on the slide: Georgie sees the egg, picks it up and finds it has gone bad, then runs away from the smell."

DO:
- Hold the book open at page 10.
- Read each panel idea aloud.
- Take 2 to 3 student responses.

TEACHER NOTES:
Guided practice using the rotten egg moment. Page 10 anchors the events. Check that students can sequence the three panels.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who muddle the order. Prompt: "What happens first? Next? Last?"
28:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "A comic strip helps us to..."
- "Pick the best answer."

DO:
- Read each option aloud.
- Cue silent think, then fingers up.
- Reveal: better understand the characters' thoughts and feelings.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers
Script:
- Ask: what does a comic strip help us do? Expected: better understand the characters' thoughts and feelings.
- Scan for: most students pointing to the same option.
PROCEED:
- >=80% correct. Move to the booklet task on slide 29.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students pick "draw the characters" because that is part of comic making.
- Reteach: drawing is a tool, but the purpose is to show feelings and thoughts.
- Re-check: ask "Why did we add thought bubbles to the comic?"

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick purpose check. Drawing is the activity, but understanding character thinking is the goal.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick the drawing answer. Quick correction: "Drawing helps us, but the comic is for the thoughts."
29:
SAY:
- "Open your booklet to the page titled Lesson 8: Understanding, responding to and creating text."
- "Make your own comic strip using the three panels."
- "Use thought bubbles or speech bubbles to show what the character is thinking or saying."

DO:
- Wait until every student has the right page open.
- Read the task heading aloud once.
- Circulate and support students who freeze on the first panel.

TEACHER NOTES:
Independent comic strip task. Use slides 25, 26 and 27 as visual references.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Use the rotten egg sequence from slide 27 as the comic.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Add a label to each panel and a title above the comic.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who only draw and do not add a thought bubble. Prompt: "What is the character thinking here?"
30:
TEACHER NOTES:
Divider for the editing focus. Reset the room: book away, boards out, eyes up. Move to slide 31 once everyone is ready.
31:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen first."
- "Editing is when we check a sentence carefully so it is correct."
- "There are three things to check."
- "A capital letter at the start. Capital letters for proper nouns. Punctuation at the end."

DO:
- Tap each line of the checklist as you say it.
- Hold up three fingers and count: start, names, end.
- Keep boards down for now.

TEACHER NOTES:
Same editing checklist as Lesson 7. Quick recap before adding sentence types.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who can repeat the words but not the actions. Prompt one student to point to the capital letter at the start of any nearby sentence.
32:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen."
- "There are four sentence types. Today we look at two: statement and question."
- "A statement tells us something. It ends with a full stop."
- "Read with me: I like to play sport."
- "A question asks us something. It ends with a question mark."
- "Questions often start with words like what, when, how, why, who, where, do, did, can, will."
- "Read with me: What time is it?"

DO:
- Point to the example sentences.
- Tap the full stop on the statement, then the question mark on the question.
- Read the trigger word list slowly.

TEACHER NOTES:
Introduces statement and question. The trigger words help students spot a question early.

WATCH FOR:
- Students using a question mark on a statement. Quick correction: "Is this asking something? No, so full stop."
33:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen."
- "Two more sentence types: command and exclamation."
- "A command tells us to do something. It ends with a full stop or an exclamation mark."
- "Read with me: Stop running!"
- "An exclamation shows strong feeling. It ends with an exclamation mark."
- "Read with me: I love this song!"
- "The editing checklist still applies to all four types."

DO:
- Tap the exclamation mark each time.
- Use a strong voice for both examples.

TEACHER NOTES:
Introduces command and exclamation. Both can use exclamation marks. Commands tell, exclamations express feeling.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing command with exclamation. Quick reminder: a command tells you to do something, an exclamation expresses feeling.
34:
SAY:
- "Read each sentence with me."
- "On your board, write S for statement, Q for question, C for command or E for exclamation."
- "Show me each one as we go."

DO:
- Read sentence one: How many books have you read?
- Wait for boards. Reveal: Q for question.
- Read sentence two: I am going to walk home today. Reveal: S for statement.
- Read sentence three: Oh no, that's terrible! Reveal: E for exclamation.
- Read sentence four: Get out of the way! Reveal: C for command.

TEACHER NOTES:
Guided practice on the four sentence types. Use the end punctuation and the meaning to decide.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick C for any sentence with an exclamation mark. Quick reminder: a command tells you to do something.
35:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen."
- "Today you will edit sentences about the characters from A Year on our Farm."
- "The characters are Mum, Dad, Jess, Georgie and the narrator."

DO:
- Point to each photo on the slide.
- Recap from slide 10 if needed: characters are people, animals or creatures who think, act and feel.

TEACHER NOTES:
Links the editing work back to the characters. Keep the focus tight on the family members.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who try to add new characters. Quick reminder: stick to the family members in the book.
36:
SAY:
- "Watch this first."
- "Read with me: jess picked fruit in january."
- "Find the nouns. Jess and January are proper nouns. Fruit is a common noun."
- "I add capitals on Jess, January and the start of the sentence."
- "I add a full stop at the end."
- "Final sentence: Jess picked fruit in January."

DO:
- Read the lowercase sentence aloud first.
- Tap each proper noun as you change it.
- Reveal the corrected sentence: Jess picked fruit in January.

TEACHER NOTES:
First worked example. Capital J on Jess. Capital J on January. Full stop. Fruit stays lowercase because it is a type, not a name.

WATCH FOR:
- Students wanting to capitalise fruit. Quick correction: "Is fruit one special fruit or any fruit? Any fruit, so no capital."
37:
SAY:
- "Read with me: georgie thinks the feet of vanessa's chicks are tickly."
- "On your board, identify the nouns and capitalise the proper nouns."
- "How do we complete the sentence?"
- "Show me your board."

DO:
- Read the lowercase sentence aloud.
- Wait while students write or underline.
- Reveal the changes: Georgie, Vanessa, capital G at the start, full stop.

TEACHER NOTES:
Guided practice. Two proper nouns: Georgie and Vanessa. Chicks and feet are common nouns.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who capitalise chicks or feet. Quick reminder: those are types, not names.
38:
SAY:
- "Read with me: dad brings home daisy for us to look after."
- "Edit this sentence using the checklist."
- "Show me your board."

DO:
- Read the lowercase sentence aloud.
- Wait silently while students edit.
- Reveal the corrections: Dad, Daisy, capital D at the start, full stop at the end.

TEACHER NOTES:
Guided practice. Dad is used as a name here, so it takes a capital. Daisy is a name, so it takes a capital.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who leave dad in lowercase. Quick reminder: when dad is being used as the name, it gets a capital.
39:
SAY:
- "Read with me: do kelly and keeper have kennels to sleep in."
- "This sentence is asking something."
- "Edit using the checklist. What punctuation goes at the end?"
- "Show me your board."

DO:
- Read the lowercase sentence with rising voice to flag the question.
- Wait for boards.
- Reveal: Kelly, Keeper, capital D at the start, question mark at the end.

TEACHER NOTES:
First question sentence to edit. The trigger word is "do" at the start. Two proper nouns: Kelly and Keeper.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who put a full stop at the end. Quick correction: "Is this sentence asking something? Yes, so question mark."
40:
SAY:
- "Read with me: don't chase the parrot maria."
- "This sentence is telling someone to stop. It is a command."
- "Edit it using the checklist. What punctuation goes at the end?"
- "Show me your board."

DO:
- Read the lowercase sentence with a strong voice.
- Wait for boards.
- Reveal: Maria, capital D at the start, exclamation mark at the end.

TEACHER NOTES:
A command sentence. Commands tell us to do something and can end with an exclamation mark for stronger feeling. Maria is the only proper noun here. Parrot stays lowercase.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who use a question mark. Quick correction: "Is this asking, or telling someone what to do?"
41:
SAY:
- "Read with me again: do kelly and keeper have kennels to sleep in."
- "Edit this sentence using the checklist."
- "Remember: it is a question."

DO:
- Read the lowercase sentence with rising voice.
- Wait for boards.
- Reveal: Kelly, Keeper, capital D at the start, question mark at the end.

TEACHER NOTES:
This slide repeats slide 39 with the same sentence. Use it for a quick recap or skip if students have already mastered it.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who lose focus on a repeated example. Use it to confirm mastery, then move on quickly.
42:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen first."
- "Pick a character from the story for your sentence."
- "Remember the characters: Mum, Dad, Jess, Georgie or the narrator."
- "The animals are important, but they are not characters in the same way as the family."

DO:
- Point to each character photo on the slide.
- Repeat the family list out loud.
- Pause for students to choose silently.

TEACHER NOTES:
Returns to the character list before independent writing. Use slide 10 if students need a quick recap.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick an animal as the character. Quick reminder: stick to the five family members.
43:
SAY:
- "Think of a sentence you could write about your character."
- "What ideas do you remember from the story?"
- "Turn and share your sentence with a partner."

DO:
- Point to each character photo on the slide.
- Give 60 seconds to think and share.
- Take 2 to 3 student sentences to share with the class.

TEACHER NOTES:
Oral rehearsal before writing. Students prepare a sentence aloud first. This raises confidence for the writing on slide 44.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Use the frame "___ likes to ___ on the farm." with a chosen character.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Write a sentence with two characters in it.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who get stuck choosing a character. Quick prompt: "Pick the character you remember best."
44:
SAY:
- "Now write the sentence you just shared."
- "Use the editing checklist on the side."
- "Capital at the start? Tick or fix."
- "Capitals for proper nouns? Tick or fix."
- "Punctuation at the end? Tick or fix."

DO:
- Read the example sentence on the slide: Mum enjoys milking Lillypilly in the milking shed.
- Give 2 to 3 minutes for writing and editing.
- Circulate and support students who freeze.

TEACHER NOTES:
First You Do for sentence writing. Students write their statement and tick or fix using the three checks.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Use the frame from the slide: "___ enjoys ___ in the ___." Replace the blanks with character and farm details.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Add a describing word, like "happy" or "cheeky," before the noun.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write the sentence but skip the checks. Prompt: "Tick each check or fix it."
45:
SAY:
- "Now write a question about a character from the story."
- "Use a question mark at the end."
- "Edit using the checklist."

DO:
- Read the example on the slide: Why does Dad use the truck to help spread the hay?
- Remind students that questions often start with what, when, how, why, who, where, do, did, can or will.
- Give 2 to 3 minutes for writing and editing.

TEACHER NOTES:
Second You Do, focused on questions. The trigger word list from slide 32 is the support tool here.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Use a sentence starter from the trigger list, like "What does ___?" or "How does ___?"
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Write two questions, each with a different starter word.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who use a full stop. Quick correction: "Is this sentence asking something? Yes, so question mark."
46:
SAY:
- "Now write a question, command or exclamation about a character."
- "Choose the punctuation that fits."
- "Edit using the checklist."

DO:
- Read the example on the slide: I can't believe that Georgie found a rotten egg!
- Remind students of the four sentence types from slides 32 and 33.
- Give 2 to 3 minutes for writing and editing.

TEACHER NOTES:
Third You Do, free choice across question, command and exclamation. Statement is not the focus on this slide.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Pick one type and use the example from the slide as a model.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
